metadata.name: watch
metadata.displayName: watch - Execute a program periodically, showing output fullscreen
metadata.description: Execute a program repeatedly and display its output

installation.note: watch is typically included in procps package, available on most Linux systems by default

overview.summary: The watch command executes a program repeatedly, displaying its output fullscreen and updating it at regular intervals. It's perfect for monitoring system resources, watching file changes, or observing the progress of long-running operations. The screen is cleared and updated each time, making it easy to spot changes.
when_to_use: Monitor system resources (CPU, memory, disk) in real-time
Watch file sizes or directory contents change
Track command output that changes over time

syntax.description: Execute COMMAND repeatedly and display its output. Default interval is 2 seconds. Press Ctrl+C to exit.

options.use_case: Change how often the command runs. Lower values update more frequently but use more CPU
Make it easier to spot what changed between updates - changed values are highlighted

options.description: Turn off the header showing the interval and command
options.use_case: Cleaner output without the header bar at the top

options.description: Beep if command has a non-zero exit code
options.use_case: Get audio alert when a condition changes (file appears, process exits, etc.)

options.description: Interpret ANSI color and style sequences
options.use_case: Preserve color output from commands that support colored output

examples.title: Monitor disk usage
examples.description: Watch disk space usage update every second
examples.output:
Every 1.0s: df -h

Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/sda1        20G   15G  4.0G  79% /
(Updates every second showing current disk usage)

output_explanation.format: Header shows interval and command, followed by command output that updates

elements.meaning: Header showing update interval (1 second) and command being executed
The actual command output that refreshes every second
The screen clears and refreshes with new data at the specified interval

output_explanation.notes: The screen updates in place - you see the same location but with fresh data. Press Ctrl+C to exit.

examples.use_case: Monitor disk space changes in real-time, useful during large file operations

examples.title: Watch process list
examples.description: Monitor Python processes, updating every 2 seconds (default)
examples.output:
Every 2.0s: ps aux | grep python

user  1234  0.5  1.2  python script.py
(Updates showing current Python processes)

output_explanation.format: Command output refreshes periodically, showing current state

elements.meaning: Default update interval (2 seconds) if not specified
Current output that changes as processes start/stop

output_explanation.notes: Useful for monitoring if a process is running, watching CPU/memory usage of processes, or seeing when processes appear/disappear.

examples.use_case: Monitor specific processes, watch for process starts/stops, track resource usage

examples.title: Highlight changes
examples.description: Monitor memory usage with differences highlighted
examples.output:
Every 2.0s: free -h

              total        used        free
Mem:           8.0G        4.2G        3.8G
(Changed values highlighted between updates)

output_explanation.format: Values that changed since last update are highlighted

elements.meaning: Numbers or text that changed since the previous update are visually highlighted
Memory statistics that update and show changes

output_explanation.notes: The -d flag makes it much easier to spot changes. Changed values stand out, making it obvious what's changing over time.

examples.use_case: Easily spot what's changing in command output, identify trends or anomalies

examples.title: Watch file listing
examples.description: Monitor the 10 newest files, updating every 0.5 seconds
examples.output:
Every 0.5s: ls -lht | head -10

-rw-r--r-- 1 user user 1.5M Jan 15 10:30 newfile.txt
(Shows newest files, updates very frequently)

output_explanation.format: Fast updates show directory changes in near real-time

elements.meaning: Update every 0.5 seconds (half a second) - very frequent updates
List files sorted by time, show only top 10
Directory contents that refresh showing newest files first

output_explanation.notes: Very useful for monitoring directory changes, watching log files appear, or tracking file creation during operations.

examples.use_case: Monitor directory changes, watch for new files, track file creation during operations

examples.title: Monitor network connections
examples.output:
Every 1.0s: netstat -tuln | grep :80

tcp  0.0.0.0:80  LISTEN
(Shows network connections on port 80, highlights when connections change)

elements.meaning: Current network connections that change over time

misconceptions.title: watch runs commands in background
misconceptions.misconception: watch runs commands as background processes that continue after watch exits
misconceptions.reality: watch executes commands in the foreground and stops when you press Ctrl+C. The commands themselves run normally but are executed repeatedly by watch.
misconceptions.tip: Press Ctrl+C to stop watch. The commands being watched are not background processes.

misconceptions.title: watch can watch files directly
misconceptions.misconception: watch can monitor file changes directly like 'watch file.txt'
misconceptions.reality: watch executes commands, not files. To watch a file, use a command: 'watch cat file.txt' or 'watch tail file.txt'
misconceptions.tip: Always provide a command to execute. For files, use commands like cat, tail, head, or ls

common_pitfalls.issue: Commands with quotes need proper escaping
common_pitfalls.description: Complex commands with quotes, pipes, or special characters can be tricky to pass to watch
common_pitfalls.solution: Use single quotes around the entire command: watch 'ps aux | grep python'. For nested quotes, escape properly or use different quote types.

common_pitfalls.issue: Too frequent updates cause high CPU usage
common_pitfalls.description: Setting interval too low (like 0.1 seconds) can consume significant CPU resources
common_pitfalls.solution: Use reasonable intervals (1-5 seconds for most cases). Only use very short intervals when necessary.

common_pitfalls.description: Some commands' color output doesn't appear in watch
common_pitfalls.solution: Use -c flag to preserve ANSI colors, or force color in the command: watch -c 'ls --color=always'

related_commands.relationship: Interactive process monitor; watch can run top commands periodically
Interactive system monitor; watch is simpler for basic periodic monitoring
Shows end of files; often used with watch to monitor log files
Loop construct; can create custom watch-like behavior in scripts

best_practices: Use -d flag to easily spot changes in output
Set appropriate intervals - 1-5 seconds for most cases, avoid very short intervals
Quote complex commands properly: watch 'command with | pipes and "quotes"'
Use -c to preserve color output from commands that support it
Combine with head/tail to limit output size for cleaner display
performance_tips: Lower intervals use more CPU - balance update frequency with resource usage
Simple commands run faster - complex pipelines add overhead on each update
For very frequent monitoring, consider specialized tools like htop or custom scripts

additional_notes.default_interval: Default update interval is 2 seconds if not specified
additional_notes.exit: Press Ctrl+C to exit watch and return to command prompt
additional_notes.fullscreen: watch uses full terminal screen, clearing it on each update
additional_notes.command_execution: Commands run in a shell, so shell features (pipes, redirection) work normally
